 Live FAA ground stop latest updates: Thousands more flights canceled Saturday; officials blame overloaded routers; no sign of cyberattack
 Airlines are working to recover from the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years, and Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage could happen again without new funding.
 Kate Murphy , Andrew Romano , Jack Brewster Updated Sat, November 14, 2026 at 3:16 PM UTC Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Travelers wait for their luggage at Los Angeles International Airport on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, in Los Angeles. (AP Photo/William Liang) (AP Photo/William Liang) Airlines canceled thousands more flights Saturday as they worked to recover from a nationwide ground stop that halted departures across the U.S. for more than four hours Friday, the longest since the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
 More than 3,800 U.S. flights were canceled Saturday and more than 2,300 were delayed as of 10:08 a.m. ET, according to FlightAware. That's on top of more than 9,100 cancellations Friday.
 The Federal Aviation Administration lifted the ground stop at 8:15 p.m. ET Friday. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a press conference Friday night that the airspace had reopened, but warned that "it'll be slow."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "It's going to take us some time to unwind what happened this afternoon," he said.
 Duffy said that "instability" in the radar communications at air traffic control centers began at 3:36 p.m. ET. More than 3,500 planes were in the air when the ground stop was issued. He blamed it on an "incredibly old air traffic system."
 "We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s little copper lines," Duffy said. "It's an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded."
 Citing multiple sources, CBS News reported that "an update to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage." It reported that the system is operated by L3Harris Technologies. L3Harris did not immediately respond to Yahoo News' request for comment.
 Advertisement Advertisement When asked if he could say with certainty that the problem wasn't caused by a cyberattack, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, "There is nothing certain right now. It doesn't appear that way." Mullin also said the outage wasn't connected to Microsoft 's global outage .
 On Friday, Duffy asked for $50 billion from Congress to modernize the nation's air traffic control system, on top of the $12.5 billion lawmakers approved last year. He also didn't rule out another outage. "You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build, and I can't wait for that," Duffy said.
 Travelers whose flights were canceled are owed a refund if they choose not to fly, and Delta and United are offering travel waivers. But a Transportation Department rule that took effect Oct. 19 says "government system failures" are no longer considered within an airline's control, which could make other compensation harder to get.
 Sen. Tammy Duckworth, a Democrat from Illinois and a ranking member of an aviation subcommittee, called for an investigation. "Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation," she wrote on X .
 Live 7 updates Sat, Nov 14, 2026 03:15 PM UTC Jack Brewster American, which canceled the most flights Friday, warns of more cancellations today
 An American Airlines aircraft lands at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in DFW Airport, Texas, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide. (AP Photo/Tony Gutierrez)
 (AP Photo/Tony Gutierrez) American Airlines is warning customers to expect more delays and cancellations Saturday as it recovers from the FAA's nationwide ground stop, CNN aviation correspondent Pete Muntean reported .
 American canceled 1,239 flights Friday, more than any other U.S. airline, according to FlightAware . Southwest canceled 1,167 flights, Delta 1,162 and United 1,137.
 The airline said the "lingering effects" of the ground stop will continue today. American said it worked through the night to reposition planes and crews. Customers can change their flights or get a refund.
 In all, more than 9,100 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were canceled Friday, FlightAware data shows.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 03:06 PM UTC Jack Brewster Duffy says ‘it is safe to fly,’ will brief reporters at 10:30 a.m.
 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday morning that air traffic operations are "slowly returning to normal" and that "it is safe to fly."
 "Planes are pushing back, taxiing, and taking off," Duffy wrote on X . He warned that travelers "will continue to see some delays and cancellations as carriers reschedule flights and reposition aircraft/crews where they are needed most."
 Duffy said he'll hold a press briefing at 10:30 a.m. ET at Transportation Department headquarters in Washington.
 The FAA urged travelers to check their flight status with their airline. Real-time airport updates are posted at nasstatus.faa.gov .

 Travelers slept in baggage claims and on benches at Washington-area airports as the nationwide ground stop and cancellations left them stuck overnight.

 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 02:54 PM UTC Jack Brewster Authors drop out of Texas Book Festival; Longhorns make it to LSU after late flight
 More than 20 authors have canceled appearances at the Texas Book Festival in Austin this weekend because of the ground stop and flight disruptions, according to the festival's updates page . The festival has called off three sessions so far.
 "The Festival is on," organizers wrote. "Sessions will continue with authors who can be present."
 The authors who canceled include Pulitzer Prize-winning historian Beverly Gage and novelists Laurie Frankel, Jim Shepard and Rachel Khong. Two authors who couldn't make it Saturday said they'd be there Sunday.
 Rebecca Bendheim, a children's author flying in from Portland, Maine, got stuck at Chicago's O'Hare International Airport. "People speaking on full speakerphone to beg hotels to take them. People crying. People yelling at the phone," she told KUT , Austin's NPR station.
 The Texas Longhorns football team had already boarded its charter to Baton Rouge for Saturday's game against LSU when the ground stop hit. The team had to get off the plane and went back to campus. It flew out after the stop was lifted and landed just before 11:30 p.m. Friday, according to The Advocate . The SEC said the game will start on time at 6:30 p.m. CT.
 Tennessee, Ole Miss, Washington, Baylor, Minnesota, Kansas State, Purdue and Tulane also couldn't fly Friday, Sports Business Journal reported.

 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 02:32 PM UTC Jack Brewster 2000s rock bands play an in-flight concert on one of the last flights out before the ground stop
 Passengers on a Southwest Airlines flight from Los Angeles to Orlando got a surprise concert Friday from three bands of the early 2000s: Hoobastank, Simple Plan and The Used.
 Hoobastank singer Doug Robb sang the band's 2004 hit "The Reason" in the aisle as passengers sang along. Simple Plan followed with "Perfect" and "I'm Just a Kid," and The Used played "The Taste of Ink," the Daily Voice reported .
 The flight was among the last to leave Los Angeles International Airport before the FAA's ground stop, passenger Jordan Orion told the Daily Voice. "We got really lucky," she said.
 All three bands are scheduled to play the Vans Warped Tour in Orlando this weekend. Southwest is the festival's airline partner and runs a "Live at 35" program that puts on pop-up performances during flights, according to Simple Flying . It's not clear whether the performances were planned.
 "Every plane was grounded today, but the emo gods made sure this one flew," musician LØLØ wrote on Instagram, in a post Hoobastank reshared.
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 02:15 PM UTC Jack Brewster What caused the ground stop: Officials point to new tech overloading old routers
 Trump administration officials said new technology being added to the nation's air traffic control system overloaded aging equipment. That caused gaps in radar and communications, which led to Friday's ground stop.
 "Our routers actually got overloaded with data," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters Friday night. The routers then began giving inconsistent data, he said, "and because of that, we shut the system down."
 Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said new security patches added to the older system appeared to "overwhelm" its routers. Asked about the patches, Duffy said, "By doing nothing, you inject way more risk into the system," according to The Verge .
 The FAA's preliminary investigation points to Cisco 600 series routers built between 2001 and 2006, senior government sources told CBS News . The sources said the faulty equipment has been identified and isolated. They also said they're getting conflicting information about the cause. Multiple sources told CBS Friday that an update to the private communications network connecting the air traffic control system caused it to reboot and crash. L3Harris Technologies operates that network and did not immediately respond to Yahoo News' request for comment.
 The FBI doesn't believe a cyberattack or criminal activity was behind the outage and is looking at a software update as a possible cause, Bloomberg reported, according to SecurityWeek .
 The airspace was operating normally by 7:30 a.m. ET Saturday, CBS reported .
 Sat, Nov 14, 2026 02:10 PM UTC Jack Brewster More than 3,600 US flights canceled Saturday as airlines dig out
 More than 3,600 flights within, into or out of the U.S. had been canceled Saturday as of 9:10 a.m. ET, and more than 1,800 had been delayed, according to FlightAware .
 Airlines are running one of their lightest schedules of the week on Saturday. They're bringing in spare planes and crews to get aircraft back where they belong, after the ground stop left many planes at the wrong airports overnight. About 3 million people would usually be scheduled to fly on a Saturday, according to aviation data firm Cirium.
 "It depends on do we have crews available, do we have pilots and flight attendants available to fly your flight," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday night. "It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened."
 American Airlines said in a statement late Friday that it was "positioning the airline for the strongest possible recovery in the days ahead."
